_doc: SPINOFF-IDEAS-1 (owner, 2026-11-17): 'use the maximum resources possible, but stay cost constrained; brainstorm new ideas automatically; keep increasing scope and loops'. Ultrastable proposes, scores and queues its own spinoffs and loop scope increases against the free-plan headroom the FREE-TIER-1 governor measures (ops/free-tier.json). Read by foundation/ideas.py; checked by `python3 -m foundation ideas --check`. Numbers are hypotheses re-tuned from settled outcomes; never edit one to clear a breach.

cadence._doc: launches per day by governor level; a stale snapshot counts as degrade

bank.name: Free-Tier Meter
bank.tagline: How much of Cloudflare's free plan does a whole autonomous system use today? Live, from the loop that spends it.
bank.showcases: the budget governor: doing the most with the least

bank.name: Ultrastable by the Numbers
bank.tagline: Loops running, edges wired, stories passing and what the system does not know yet, straight from its own ledger.

bank.name: What Changed
bank.tagline: Every change the system made to itself, by who or what originated it. No person in the path.
bank.showcases: provenance: where every change came from

bank.name: Loop Ledger
bank.tagline: How many closed loops keep this system running, and which ones are on a clock.

bank.name: Spinoff Portfolio
bank.tagline: The apps Ultrastable launched on its own, what they cost and how many it retired.
bank.showcases: autonomous idea-to-app launching with a portfolio manager

bank.name: security.txt Writer
bank.tagline: Answer three choices, get a ready RFC 9116 security.txt. Closes the gap Blindspot Check finds.
bank.showcases: check, fix, re-check: the loop closed for a stranger

bank.name: SPF and DMARC Writer
bank.tagline: Pick your mail provider, get the exact SPF and DMARC records to publish.
bank.showcases: check, fix, re-check: the loop closed for a stranger

bank.name: Plain Privacy Page Draft
bank.tagline: A few choices become a plain-language privacy page draft. Not legal advice; says so.
bank.showcases: blind-spot register turned into a product

bank.name: Country Snapshot
bank.tagline: Type a country code, see its latest World Bank figures for electricity, drinking water, internet use and literacy.
bank.showcases: an open public-data dashboard for any country
bank.need_evidence: The World Bank publishes these for 200+ economies; gaps in basic services are the core development measures. Need is a stated judgment.

context.decider: Nobody pays: readers choose it themselves. The people it describes (residents of each country) are mostly not its readers, so it must not be pitched as a service to them.
context.problem: The stated problem is finding a country's latest basic-service figures quickly; it shows the World Bank numbers and links the source, and claims nothing about fixing the gaps.
context.infrastructure: Pages are plain HTML under 30 KB with no script needed to read the answer, so they load on a cheap phone over a slow 2G or 3G link; free to use, with no account, app or data plan beyond one page.
context.misuse: Figures can be quoted without their year or used to rank countries unfairly; each number shows its year and source link, and the page states that gaps are measures, not judgments.

pilot.size: One page with four indicators, live since launch, with use counted per lookup and no identity stored.
pilot.feedback: Uses per week and lookups that return no data are read by the spinoff loop each day.
pilot.scale_when: More indicators only after uses_7d holds above zero for four weeks and empty-lookup rate stays under ten percent.

context.builds_on: Builds on the World Bank open data people and journalists already cite, instead of a new dataset of our own.

bank.name: Air Quality Check
bank.tagline: Type a city anywhere, see its air quality right now and the current particle levels, from open forecast data.
bank.need_evidence: Outdoor air pollution is a leading environmental cause of early death worldwide per WHO. Need is a stated judgment.

context.decider: Readers choose it themselves and nobody pays; people with asthma, parents and outdoor workers are the people served and the readers at once.
context.problem: The stated problem is knowing whether the air is bad right now; it answers that and does not claim to clean the air or replace official alerts.
context.infrastructure: Pages are plain HTML under 30 KB with no script needed to read the answer, so they load on a cheap phone over a slow 2G or 3G link; free to use, with no account, app or data plan beyond one page.
context.misuse: A forecast model can be wrong locally, and a reader could skip an official alert because this page looked fine; the page names the model source and tells readers to follow local official alerts first.

pilot.size: One lookup page for any city, live, with use counted per lookup and no identity stored.
pilot.feedback: Uses per week and failed city lookups are read daily by the spinoff loop.
pilot.scale_when: Alerts or history are added only after four weeks of steady use and failed lookups under ten percent.

context.builds_on: Builds on open forecast data and the air quality index scale people already see in weather apps and news.

bank.name: Quake Watch
bank.tagline: Significant earthquakes anywhere in the world this week, read live from the USGS, with a link to each event page.
bank.showcases: global hazard awareness from open data
bank.need_evidence: Earthquakes strike on every continent; the feed is worldwide. Need is a stated judgment.

context.decider: Readers choose it themselves and nobody pays; it serves people curious or worried about recent quakes.
context.problem: The stated problem is seeing this week's significant quakes in one list; it shows the USGS feed and links each event, and is not an early warning.
context.infrastructure: Pages are plain HTML under 30 KB with no script needed to read the answer, so they load on a cheap phone over a slow 2G or 3G link; free to use, with no account, app or data plan beyond one page.
context.misuse: Someone could read it as a warning system or spread fear after a quake; the page says plainly it lists past events only and links national agencies for warnings.

pilot.size: One feed page, live, use counted per load with no identity stored.
pilot.feedback: Uses per week are read daily by the spinoff loop.
pilot.scale_when: Regional filters come only after four weeks of steady use.

context.builds_on: Builds on the USGS feed that news desks and agencies already use and trust.

bank.name: Access Check
bank.tagline: Name any website, get a plain read of basic accessibility signals on its home page: language, alt text, labels, zoom.
bank.need_evidence: WHO estimates about 1.3 billion people live with a significant disability; inaccessible sites exclude them. Need is a stated judgment.

context.decider: Site owners and developers decide to fix a site; the people served are disabled visitors, who are not the ones running the check.
context.problem: The stated problem is a quick read of basic accessibility signals; it reports those few signals and says a full audit needs real users and assistive technology.
context.infrastructure: Pages are plain HTML under 30 KB with no script needed to read the answer, so they load on a cheap phone over a slow 2G or 3G link; free to use, with no account, app or data plan beyond one page.
context.misuse: A pass on four signals could be used to claim a site is accessible; the result says it checks only four basics and is not a compliance verdict.

pilot.size: Four checks on a home page, live, use counted per check with no identity stored.
pilot.feedback: Uses per week and fetch failures are read daily by the spinoff loop.
pilot.scale_when: More checks only after four weeks of steady use and fetch failures under ten percent.

context.builds_on: Builds on WCAG, the standard site owners already work to, rather than a new scoring scheme.

bank.name: Base Rates
bank.need_evidence: Kahneman and Tversky's planning fallacy and Flyvbjerg's reference-class forecasting: people judge from the inside view and ignore how such things usually go. Need is a stated judgment.
bank.tagline: Before you decide, see what usually happens: graded base rates for life, work and policy choices, and your own forecasting record.
bank.thesis: People and institutions predict from the story in front of them and ignore how often such things usually go; showing the reference class first makes forecasts better.
bank.corpus: An encyclopedia of reference classes (new businesses surviving five years, megaprojects on budget, diets kept after a year, reforms delivering their stated aim), each with its base rate, source and grade.
bank.loop: An hourly beat re-reads each entry's source series for new releases and surfaces newer studies; readers' guesses before the reveal measure which base rates surprise most and order the site.
bank.returns: A reader keeps a private forecasting record in their own browser, sees how calibrated they are, and comes back when a base rate they followed moves.
horizon: encyclopedia of 50 graded base rates with guess-first entries
decision companion: name a plan, get its reference class and a pre-mortem
bank.hook: Guess first: how often do new restaurants survive five years? Then the base rate, and how far off you were. Every person misses some, and the miss is the hook.
bank.public_good: People and governments make better decisions about money, health and policy when they see how such things usually go; it counters overconfident plans that waste public money.

context.decider: Readers choose it themselves; teachers or newsrooms may point others to it, so entries must hold up for a skeptical editor, not only a curious reader.
context.problem: The stated problem is deciding from the inside view; each entry shows the reference class and its rate before any advice, and does not tell people what to choose.
context.infrastructure: Pages are plain HTML under 30 KB with no script needed to read the answer, so they load on a cheap phone over a slow 2G or 3G link; free to use, with no account, app or data plan beyond one page.
context.misuse: A base rate can be used to talk someone out of a sound plan or to stereotype a group; entries say a rate is a starting point, show its range and source, and never rate people by group.

pilot.size: Start with ten entries, at least four drawn from sources outside the US and Europe.
pilot.feedback: Each entry records guesses before the reveal and a 'this looks wrong' tap, with nothing that identifies the reader.
pilot.scale_when: Grow toward fifty entries only after the first ten have a month of guesses and every 'looks wrong' tap is answered by a re-check.

context.builds_on: Builds on published reference-class studies and official statistics people already trust, and on the habit of asking 'how often does this work?'.

bank.name: Did It Work?
bank.need_evidence: Most public programmes are announced with stated aims and rarely judged against them; evaluations arrive years later and few people see them. Need is a stated judgment.
bank.tagline: Every big policy promised something. See what it promised, what the evaluations found since, and how the verdict moved.
bank.thesis: Policies are judged by their announcements, not their results; holding each one to its own stated aim, as evaluations arrive, changes how people argue about the next one.
bank.corpus: A casebook of policies and programmes worldwide, each with its stated aim in its own words, the evaluations published since, graded by design, and a running verdict.
bank.loop: A daily beat searches open evaluation and trial registries for each case, adds new evaluations, re-grades the verdict when evidence piles up, and logs every change of verdict with its reason.
bank.returns: Readers follow cases and see what changed since their last visit; a verdict that moved is the reason to come back.
horizon: casebook of 40 policies with stated aims and graded evaluations
verdict history and follow on any case
prediction market of the system's own: forecast the next evaluation, scored when it lands
bank.hook: Guess the verdict: did this famous policy deliver what it promised? Then the evaluations. The surprise, either way, is the hook.
bank.public_good: Citizens, journalists and staff can hold policy to its own promises, so public money moves to what works; it empowers voters with evidence.

context.decider: Readers choose it themselves; journalists and public staff are likely heavy users, and governments whose policies are graded may push back, so every verdict cites its evaluations.
context.problem: The stated problem is that policies are judged by announcements; each case shows the stated aim and the evaluations, and does not argue for or against the policy itself.
context.infrastructure: Pages are plain HTML under 30 KB with no script needed to read the answer, so they load on a cheap phone over a slow 2G or 3G link; free to use, with no account, app or data plan beyond one page.
context.misuse: A verdict can be cherry-picked to attack or defend a government; each case shows every graded evaluation found, the grade, and the date the verdict last moved, and says when evidence is thin.

pilot.size: Start with eight cases, at least half from outside the US and Europe, before the casebook grows.
pilot.feedback: Each case carries a 'this verdict looks wrong' tap and the guess-first count, with nothing that identifies the reader; every tap queues a re-check of that case.
pilot.scale_when: Grow toward forty cases only after the first eight have a month of reader guesses and every 'looks wrong' tap has been re-checked.

context.builds_on: Builds on evaluations governments and researchers already publish (3ie, J-PAL, national audit offices) instead of our own judgments.

bank.name: Open Questions
bank.need_evidence: Public writing presents settled science and open questions in the same voice; readers cannot tell what is still unknown. Need is a stated judgment.
bank.tagline: What science honestly does not know yet: the big open questions, where the evidence leans today, and how that lean has moved.
bank.thesis: Knowing what is not yet known is as useful as knowing what is; a map of open questions, with where the evidence leans and how fast it moves, is missing from public knowledge.
bank.corpus: An atlas of open questions by field, each with the competing answers, the best evidence for each, a graded lean and a history of how the lean moved.
bank.loop: A weekly beat watches review and preprint feeds for each question, files new evidence on the entry and moves the lean only when graded evidence moves it, recording why.
bank.returns: Readers record their own lean and see questions move toward an answer; a question that closes becomes an Unlearn or Practical Solutions entry.
horizon: atlas of 30 open questions with graded leans
links into Unlearn and Practical Solutions when a question settles
bank.hook: Pick your lean on a live question, then see where the evidence leans and how it moved. Knowing you hold a minority view, or that nobody knows yet, is the hook.
bank.public_good: Honest public knowledge of what is not known protects people from false certainty and points students and funders at questions worth answering.

context.decider: Readers choose it themselves; students and funders may use it to pick topics, so leans must be graded and dated.
context.problem: The stated problem is that open and settled science read the same; it marks what is open and where evidence leans, without claiming to settle it.
context.infrastructure: Pages are plain HTML under 30 KB with no script needed to read the answer, so they load on a cheap phone over a slow 2G or 3G link; free to use, with no account, app or data plan beyond one page.
context.misuse: A lean could be quoted as settled fact or used to cast doubt on settled science; each entry shows its grade, the competing answers and a plain line on what is not in question.

pilot.size: Start with six questions across different fields.
pilot.feedback: Readers record their own lean and can tap 'this lean looks wrong', with nothing that identifies them; each tap queues a re-check.
pilot.scale_when: Grow toward thirty only after the first six have a month of reader leans and every tap has been re-checked.

context.builds_on: Builds on review articles and preprint servers researchers already read, not a new source of claims.

scope_templates.title: Implement the template-generator archetype in the spinoff Worker so the queued writers (security.txt, SPF/DMARC, privacy page) can launch
scope_templates.why: three queued ideas with the highest impact are blocked only by this archetype; it adds no storage and no model calls

scope_templates.title: Collect every live app's metrics twice a day instead of once
scope_templates.why: more measurement points per app for the portfolio manager at a few requests

scope_templates.title: Refresh every status board's facts on each loop run, not only on launch
scope_templates.why: boards stay current for free; the bundle is rebuilt from committed files

scope_templates.title: Check every live app against its own claims once a day
scope_templates.why: words match code at the cost of a request per claim

scope_templates.why: neuron headroom is the least used free resource

benefit._doc: BENEFIT-1 (Rowan, 2026-11-18: 'How are you measuring public benefit?'). Public-benefit score of an idea = scale * region * need * use, then divided by (1 + cost_penalty * cost_share) like every idea. region: how many people in how many places it can serve (global or 3+ regions 1.0, two regions 0.7, one country 0.4). need: 1-5 size of the unmet need, a stated hypothesis with its evidence in the idea. use: measured, 0.5 to 1.5 from the app's uses_7d once the metrics ledger has it; unmeasured is 1.0, never zero. Hypotheses re-tuned from settled outcomes; never edit a number to clear a breach.

depth._doc: DEPTH-1 (Rowan, 2026-11-22: 'Where do you go with an air quality app? ... I want new apps that have the depth of idea, the depth of concept of Unlearn and Practical Solutions.'). What makes Unlearn and Practical Solutions deep, as fields an idea must carry before it may launch: a thesis about the world it keeps testing, a corpus that grows, a loop that keeps changing it, a reason a person returns, and a horizon of at least three phases. A single lookup, board or template is a cheap thrill: it scores nothing on depth, is refused at launch and is retired if live. Read by foundation/ideas.py depth(); checked by `ideas --check`; applied by `ideas --retire-shallow --apply`. Rowan, 2026-11-22: 'what's the hook ... what keeps people interested and engaged and sticky' and 'this is about some kind of public good, something that empowers change ... go get Squarespace if you want e-commerce': hook and public_good are required, and commerce is refused outright.

fields.thesis: the substantive claim or question about the world the app keeps testing (Unlearn: popular beliefs the evidence contradicts)
fields.corpus: the body of knowledge that grows entry by entry (Practical Solutions: solutions that worked, by problem)
fields.loop: what changes the corpus every week without a person: new evidence, new cases, new data, and how it is re-graded
fields.returns: why a person comes back: their own record, a verdict that moved, a follow-up, something new since the last visit
fields.horizon: at least three phases with a direction, so the app has somewhere to go
fields.hook: the first moment that pulls a person in and makes them care, like the Unlearn quiz: guess first, then the reveal (an app that tells people what they already know has no hook)
fields.public_good: the public good it serves and the change it empowers, in the spirit of QNFO's mission; never commerce
fields.change: the evidence-based moves (at least 3 from doctrine/change-methods.json, covering notice, update and act) that carry a person from the fact to a changed belief to an action, because humans are the weak link

aliases._doc: IDEA-BANK-1 shape (doctrine/idea-bank.json depth.corpus, depth.method, depth.returns) reads through the same rule

context_fit._doc: CONTEXT-FIT-1 (Rowan, 2026-11-23). Lessons from designs made far from the people they were for (John Mauriello's talk, as summarized by Rowan; the talk's figures are his input, not checked here): NeoNurture failed because the buyers were health ministries, not the mechanics it was built for; PlayPump solved pumping when the problem was water; free bed nets became fishing nets; OLPC dropped the hand crank where schools had no power and refused pilots; Liter of Light worked because it used bottles, water and roofs people already had. Every public-benefit idea (one with regions) answers each check in its own `context` block. Score is multiplied by floor + (1 - floor) * answered/6. A failed check in hold_on keeps the idea out of launch. ideas --check fails a live or seed idea with any check unanswered. Metric context_fit_share, target 1.0.

checks.question: Who decides to use or pay for it, and is that a different person from the one it serves?
Does it solve the problem people state, not a more interesting neighbour of it?
Does it work on the power, bandwidth, devices, skills and budget the people it serves really have, and is it cheaper than what they use now?
How will people adapt or misuse it, and what harm follows?
What small pilot with feedback from the people served comes before scale? (size, feedback, scale_when)
What do people already use and trust that it builds on, instead of replacing it with an import?
